title: A feature, a label and lost information
objectives: Measure what a feature tells us about a label, and see why processing a feature can never add information.

screens.prose: A filter sees 150 emails, 75 of them spam: 1 bit of doubt about each label. Three features are counted against the label.
screens.question: Which feature tells us most about whether an email is spam?

options.text: Whether the sender is in contacts
options.why: It helps: 55 against 20 each way. But the links rows are more lopsided, 40 to 5 and 5 to 45.
Its rows, 25 to 30 and 50 to 45, are nearly the same as the label's 50 to 50.

hints.text: A useless feature has rows that split 50 to 50 like the label.
Look for rows far from 50 to 50.
Links rows run 40 to 5 and 5 to 45.

feedback.correct: Links: its rows are the most lopsided.
feedback.generic: Not quite. Which feature's rows look least like a 50 to 50 split?

explain.text: The features carry 0.328, 0.163 and 0.003 bits about the label, out of 1. A feature informs when its rows split the label unevenly.

screens.prose: For links, the label's entropy in each row is 0.503, 0.994 and 0.469 bits. The rows hold 45, 55 and 50 emails. Their weighted average is $H(\text{label} \mid \text{links})$.
screens.question: What is $I(\text{links}; \text{label})$, in bits? Give a decimal to 3 places.

hints.text: The weighted average of the row entropies is about 0.672.
Subtract from $H(\text{label}) = 1$.

feedback.generic: Not quite. Weigh the row entropies by the row shares, then subtract from 1.

byKey.left: That is the doubt left. The information is $1 - 0.672$.
byKey.unweighted: You averaged the three rows equally. Weigh them by 45, 55 and 50 out of 150.

explain.text: $0.3 \times 0.503 + 0.367 \times 0.994 + 0.333 \times 0.469 \approx 0.672$ bits are left, so the links feature removes 0.328 of the label's 1 bit.

screens.prose: An engineer simplifies the links feature to two values: "0 to 4 links" and "5 or more". The first two rows merge into one row of 70 and 30.
screens.question: What is the mutual information of the merged feature with the label? Give a decimal to 3 places.

hints.text: The merged row is 70 not spam, 30 spam.
Weigh by $\tfrac23$ and $\tfrac13$, then subtract from 1.

feedback.correct: About 0.256 bits: merging lost 0.072 bits about spam.
feedback.generic: Not quite. The new rows are 70 to 30 (100 emails) and 5 to 45 (50 emails).

byKey.same: Merging changed the feature, and the rows 40 to 5 and 30 to 25 were not alike. Something was lost.

explain.text: Rows 70 to 30 and 5 to 45 have entropies 0.881 and 0.469, so $1 - (\tfrac23 \times 0.881 + \tfrac13 \times 0.469) \approx 0.256$ bits. The merge threw away the difference between 0 to 1 and 2 to 4 links.

screens.prose: A fair bit $X$ is copied to $Y$, but the copy flips with chance 0.1. Then $Y$ is copied to $Z$ the same way.
screens.question: What is $I(X; Y)$, in bits? Give a decimal to 3 places.

hints.text: $I(X; Y) = H(Y) - H(Y \mid X)$.
Given $X$, the flip leaves $H(0.1, 0.9)$ of doubt.
Work out $1 - 0.469$.

feedback.generic: Not quite. Given $X$, $Y$ is right with 0.9 and flipped with 0.1.

byKey.left: That is the doubt left about $Y$. Subtract it from 1.
byKey.rate: That is the chance the copy is right.

explain.text: $H(Y) = 1$ and $H(Y \mid X) = H(0.1, 0.9) \approx 0.469$, so $I(X; Y) \approx 0.531$ bits.

screens.prose: $Z$ differs from $X$ when exactly one of the two copies flips: $0.1 \times 0.9 + 0.9 \times 0.1 = 0.18$.
screens.question: What is $I(X; Z)$, in bits? Give a decimal to 3 places.

hints.text: Given $X$, $Z$ is flipped with chance 0.18.
Work out $1 - 0.680$.

byKey.squared: You squared the step's 0.531 bits. Information does not multiply along a chain; work from the 0.18 flip.
byKey.same: The second copy adds noise, so $Z$ knows less about $X$ than $Y$ does.

explain.text: $H(0.18, 0.82) \approx 0.680$, so $I(X; Z) \approx 0.320 < I(X; Y) \approx 0.531$. Each noisy copy can only lose information about $X$.

screens.prose: Every time, a step that used only the previous variable lost information. This is the **data processing inequality**: if $Z$ is computed from $Y$ alone, with or without noise, then $$I(X; Z) \le I(X; Y).$$ Merging buckets and noisy copying are both such steps.
screens.question: A feature $Y$ carries 0.3 bits about a label $X$. A model turns $Y$ into a score $Z$ using only $Y$. What can $I(X; Z)$ be?

options.text: More than 0.3 bits, if the model is clever
options.why: The model sees only $Y$, so $Z$ cannot know more about $X$ than $Y$ does.
A one-to-one score keeps 0.3; a merge or noise loses some. So 0.3 is the ceiling, not a rule.

feedback.correct: Processing keeps at most the 0.3 bits that $Y$ had.
feedback.generic: Not quite. Can $Z$ know more than its only input?

explain.text: $Z$ depends on $X$ only through $Y$, so $I(X; Z) \le I(X; Y) = 0.3$. A one-to-one score keeps all 0.3 bits.

screens.prose: A colleague builds features from the links count: its square, the log of one plus the count, and a flag for "more than 3". He says the new features add information about spam.
screens.question: Can they hold more information about the label than the links count itself?

options.text: No: each is computed from the count alone
Yes: three new features must add up to more
options.why: Each is a function of the same count. None can hold more than the count holds.

options.text: Yes: the log spreads the values out
options.why: Spreading values is one-to-one: it keeps the information, it does not add any.

hints.text: Where does each new feature get its value?
Only from the links count.
So each is processing of the count.

feedback.correct: Processing can make a feature easier to use, never more informative.
feedback.generic: Not quite. What does each new feature depend on?

byKey.yes-many: You counted features, not information. All three are processed from one count.

explain.text: By the data processing inequality, $I(\text{label}; f(\text{links})) \le I(\text{label}; \text{links})$ for every $f$. A model may still find a transformed feature easier to use.

screens.prose: The links feature's three values are renamed: "0 to 1" becomes A, "2 to 4" becomes B and "5 or more" becomes C. Nothing else changes.
screens.question: What is the mutual information of the renamed feature with the label?

options.text: Less: renaming is processing, which loses information
options.why: Renaming one to one can be undone, so nothing is lost: the inequality holds both ways.
Mutual information sees only which emails share a value, not the names of the values.

hints.text: Does the renaming merge any rows?
No: three values stay three values.
The same rows give the same entropies.

feedback.correct: A one-to-one relabelling keeps every bit.
feedback.generic: Not quite. Can the renaming be undone?

explain.text: Renaming is processing, so $I$ cannot rise; it can be undone, so $I$ cannot fall either. The table's rows are the same, only their labels change.

widget.how: Check runs 5 hidden tests on planted columns, the merged links feature, the three email features and a tie. Each result must equal the expected list exactly.

mutants.symptom: Ranks the least informative feature first.
Ties are left in the order of the dict instead of by name.

hints.text: Write a helper `mi(xs, ys)` from `Counter(xs)`, `Counter(ys)` and `Counter(zip(xs, ys))`.
Each pair adds $\tfrac{c}{n}\log_2 \tfrac{c\,n}{c_x c_y}$.
Sort names with `key=lambda name: (-mi(...), name)`.

feedback.correct: Your ranking puts the most informative feature first and breaks ties by name.
feedback.generic: Some tests failed. Read the first failing row.

byKey.error: Your code stopped with an error. Check that every value is counted with its label.
byKey.test-2: Test 2 has two equal columns. Break the tie by name: "a" before "b".
byKey.test-3: Test 3 compares links with its merged version. Merging cannot add information.

explain.text:
Sort on the pair (minus the information, name): the minus puts the largest first and the name breaks ties.

```python
return sorted(columns, key=lambda name: (-mi(columns[name], labels), name))
```

screens.prose: A quant buckets a continuous signal into four bins and counts next-day signs. The four bins carry 0.0131 bits about the sign. She wants two bins: low against high, or extreme against middle.
screens.question: How many bits does the low-against-high binning keep? Give a decimal to 4 places.

widget.label: Mutual information
widget.accept: 0.0085, from the rows 78 to 97 and 97 to 78.

hints.text: High bins: 97 up, 78 down.
Work out $I$ of the 2 by 2 table of counts.

feedback.correct: About 0.0085 bits; the extreme-against-middle binning keeps 0, since its rows are both 50 to 50.
feedback.generic: Not quite. Merge very low with low, and high with very high, then work out $I$.

byKey.four: That is the four-bin figure. Merging can only lose information.
byKey.extreme: That is the other binning: extremes 75 to 75, middles 100 to 100.

explain.text: Low against high gives rows 78 to 97 and 97 to 78: about 0.0085 bits. Extreme against middle gives 75 to 75 and 100 to 100: 0 bits about the sign. Binning can only lose information, never add it; choose bins that keep what matters.

ideas: A feature's information about a label is $I = H(\text{label}) - H(\text{label} \mid \text{feature})$: links carry 0.328 of the spam label's 1 bit.
Data processing inequality: if $Z$ is computed from $Y$ alone, $I(X; Z) \le I(X; Y)$. Merging buckets and noisy copies can lose information.
A one-to-one relabelling keeps every bit; how a signal is binned decides how much of its information survives.

formula.name: Data processing inequality
formula.tex: X \to Y \to Z \implies I(X; Z) \le I(X; Y)

summary.trap: Believing a clever transformation of a feature can create information about the label.

quiz.prose: A label $X$, a feature $Y$ with $I(X; Y) = 0.2$ bits, and a rounded version $Z$ of $Y$.
quiz.question: Which is possible?

options.why: Rounding is processing of $Y$, so $Z$ cannot know more than 0.2 bits.

feedback.generic: Not quite. Recall the data processing inequality.

explain.text: $Z$ is computed from $Y$ alone, so $0 \le I(X; Z) \le 0.2$ bits.

quiz.prose: A fair bit is copied with a flip chance of 0.2.
quiz.question: How much information does the copy keep, in bits? Give a decimal to 3 places.

byKey.rate: That is the chance the copy is right.

explain.text: $H(0.2, 0.8) \approx 0.722$, so the copy keeps about 0.278 of the 1 bit.

quiz.prose: A three-bucket feature carries 0.12 bits about a label. Its buckets are renamed 1, 2, 3 to 3, 1, 2.
quiz.question: How much does the renamed feature carry?

options.why: A renaming merges nothing and can be undone, so nothing is lost.
The buckets still split the emails the same way.

feedback.generic: Not quite. Does renaming merge any buckets?

explain.text: The rows of the table are only reordered, so every entropy, and $I$, is unchanged.
